summary: The as-cast 0Cr strip is the Cr-free member of a Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-xCr (x = 0, 3, 6, 9 wt%) austenitic low-density steel series, produced by centrifugal casting under a near-rapid solidification condition (copper mold, 600 r/min, Ar, maximum cooling rate ≈5×10^3 K/s) into 2.5 mm thick strips and left without any post-solidification heat treatment. It is a two-phase austenite (γ) + δ-ferrite strip (10.2 vol% rod-like ferrite) with nano-scale κ-carbides in the austenite, and it serves as the reference baseline for determining how Cr addition changes carbide precipitation, dislocation density and the strength–ductility balance of these near-net-shape strips.
composition: Nominal composition Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C (wt%), i.e. the Cr-free end member of the Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-xCr (x = 0, 3, 6, 9) series. The measured composition (ICP, Table 1) of the 0Cr strip is Fe balance, 26.6 wt% Mn, 9.1 wt% Al, 1.2 wt% C and no Cr (reported as "–"). Fe is the base element; the high Mn and C contents were chosen to stabilize austenite and to provide C solid-solution strengthening plus κ-carbide precipitation strengthening, while the high Al content is the source of the low density. The charge was prepared from high-purity Fe (99.99%), Mn (99.9%), Al (99.9%), C (99.8%) and Cr (99.9%).
processing: Centrifugal casting under a near-rapid solidification condition (process lineage: induction melting → centrifugal casting into a rotating copper mold → as-cast strip). An alloy ingot was reheated to melt by an induction coil; the liquid metal was then poured into a copper mold rotating at 600 r/min in an Ar atmosphere, giving a calculated maximum cooling rate of about 5×10^3 K/s. The resulting strip size was (60–80) mm × 60 mm × 2.5 mm. This as-cast strip is the un-annealed terminal condition of the sample: it received no post-solidification heat treatment (in the same study, sibling strips were annealed in vacuum at 550 °C for 5 h for comparison).
microstructure: Two-phase microstructure of austenite (γ) plus δ-ferrite, in which austenite is the major, continuous matrix phase (FCC; γ reflections (111), (200), (220), (311), (222) in XRD; austenite lattice constant 3.70 Å) and δ-ferrite occurs as rod-like particles uniformly dispersed in the austenite, quantitatively measured at 10.2 vol%. All ferrite particles lie at the centres of austenite grains, indicating that δ-ferrite first nucleated and grew from the melt during near-rapid solidification, consistent with the FA (ferrite-to-austenite) solidification mode L → L+δ → L+δ+γ → δ+γ. The 0Cr strip has the weakest δ(110) XRD intensity of the series, i.e. the lowest ferrite content. Nano-scale κ-carbide precipitates are present in the austenite: a clear {100}-type κ-carbide superlattice is seen in the [001]γ+[001]κ SADP, and the average κ-carbide diameter in the as-cast 0Cr strip is 8 nm. Because the κ-carbides in the austenite are too small to resolve, they are only imaged in dark field at the austenite/ferrite phase boundary. The austenite contains only a few dislocations (i.e. a comparatively low dislocation density), and the phase interface set present is austenite/δ-ferrite.
properties: Tensile properties (gauge 20 mm × 4 mm × 1 mm, strain rate 1×10^-3 s^-1, MTS Criterion Model 44 with 10 kN capacity, values averaged over 3 measurements, each supported by more than three specimens): yield strength 724 ± 16 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 924 ± 24 MPa, total elongation 40.8 ± 8 %, and an average steady-stage strain-hardening rate of 1626 MPa — the lowest of the four strips (1626, 2048, 2266, 2385 MPa for 0Cr, 3Cr, 6Cr, 9Cr). The 0Cr strip is the most ductile as-cast strip of the series (largest elongation) but has among the lowest UTS. Measured average density 6.49 g/cm³ (SJ-600G Electronic Water Displacement Density Analyzer). Post-fracture deformation structure: average slip-band spacing ≈90 nm and average slip-band width 13.4 nm in the austenite. Characterization techniques applied to this sample: ICP mass spectrometry for composition, XRD (D/Max-2200, Cu target, 40 kV/40 mA, 4°/min) for phase identification, optical microscopy (Zeiss Axio imager A2m) for ferrite fraction and morphology, TEM (JEM-2100F, 200 kV) in bright field, dark field and SADP for dislocations, κ-carbides and slip bands, and uniaxial tensile testing.
mechanisms: Near-rapid solidification (calculated maximum cooling rate ≈5×10^3 K/s, copper mold at 600 r/min) solidifies the Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C melt in the FA mode, L → L+δ → L+δ+γ → δ+γ, so δ-ferrite nucleates and grows first from the melt and all ferrite particles end up at the centres of austenite grains.

The 26.6 wt% Mn and 1.2 wt% C contents stabilize the austenite matrix and provide C solid-solution strengthening plus κ-carbide precipitation strengthening, while the 9.1 wt% Al is responsible for the reduced density (6.49 g/cm³) of the Cr-free strip.

Rapid cooling inevitably generates thermal stress in the strip, which produces dislocations; in the Cr-free 0Cr strip only a few dislocations are found in the austenite because the abundant κ-carbide precipitation on cooling limits dislocation formation (the opposite trend is seen in Cr-containing strips where κ-carbides are suppressed).

Nano-scale κ-carbides (~8 nm average diameter in the as-cast 0Cr strip) obstruct dislocation glide; a dislocation that has sheared a κ-carbide is easily cut through by following dislocations, so shearing becomes localized and the resulting glide-plane softening effect yields the low steady-stage strain-hardening rate (1626 MPa) of the as-cast Cr-free strip.

Because the relatively large κ-carbides in the 0Cr strip obstruct dislocations strongly, shear localizes and the average spacing between slip bands after tensile fracture is comparatively wide (~90 nm), whereas the smaller and less abundant κ-carbides in the 6Cr strip allow multi-directional shearing and a narrower slip-band spacing (~80 nm).

The low initial dislocation density of the as-cast 0Cr strip, together with its wide slip-band structure, allows it to reach the highest total elongation (40.8 %) among the as-cast strips, showing that initial dislocation density — not only the ability to form slip bands during deformation — controls ductility in this austenitic low-density steel.

Annealing at 550 °C for 5 h promotes further κ-carbide precipitation and growth in the Cr-free strip (XRD κ(111) peak at ~41.4°, average carbide diameter growing to ~14 nm); since dislocations can only pass through κ-carbides smaller than about 10 nm, the coarser carbides become barriers, fewer slip bands form and the total elongation of the 0Cr strip drops to ~30.1 %, accompanied by a yield-strength increase of +158 MPa.

Slip-band width is inversely correlated with slip-band spacing (dynamic slip-band refinement, DSBR): finer slip bands with smaller spacing normally accompany higher ductility, but in the 0Cr/6Cr comparison this relationship is disturbed by differences in initial dislocation density.
conclusions: As the Cr-free reference of the near-rapidly solidified Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-xCr (x = 0, 3, 6, 9) strip series, the as-cast 0Cr strip establishes the baseline behaviour against which the Cr effect is judged. It has the lowest δ-ferrite fraction (10.2 vol%) and the strongest κ-carbide precipitation (clear superlattice, ~8 nm carbides), the fewest dislocations, the lowest steady-stage strain-hardening rate (1626 MPa) and the highest total elongation (40.8 %) of the as-cast strips, with YS 724 ± 16 MPa and UTS 924 ± 24 MPa. Cr addition increases the ferrite fraction, suppresses κ-carbide precipitation, raises the dislocation density and, at 9 wt% Cr, produces grain-boundary Cr23C6 instead of κ-carbides; this makes the yield strength of as-cast strips first fall (617 MPa at 3Cr) and then rise above the Cr-free value (740 MPa at 9Cr) while total elongation decreases monotonically (40.8 → 33.2 → 31.6 → 20.3 %). Annealing at 550 °C for 5 h raises the yield strength of all strips through more carbide precipitation, but the Cr-free strip uniquely loses ductility (TE 40.8 → 30.1 %, −10.7 %) whereas the Cr-containing strips gain ductility because of dislocation recovery; consequently the annealed 6Cr strip is more ductile than the annealed Cr-free strip. The results show that κ-carbide content/size and initial dislocation density must be balanced to reach a good strength–ductility combination in these low-density steel strips.
unmapped: In Cr-containing (3, 6, 9 wt%) strips annealed at 550 °C for 5 h, grain boundaries and the dendritic structure could not be revealed by SEM under the same conditions in which they were clearly observed in the annealed 0Cr strip; the authors attribute this to Cr improving the corrosion resistance of the strips.

Prolonging the 550 °C anneal of the Cr-containing 3Cr strip from 1 h to 9 h gradually removed dislocations and increased plasticity while yield strength stayed nearly constant after 1 h, indicating that κ-carbides precipitate mainly within the first hour and that recovery needs longer time; this time-series analysis was performed on the 3Cr sibling, not on the 0Cr sample.
